text: We have been born into a monarchy: our liberty is to obey God.
author: Seneca

text: I am not a wise man, and I will not be one in order to feed your spite: so do not require me to be on a level with the best of men, but merely to be better than the worst: I am satisfied, if every day I take away something from my vices and correct my faults.
author: Seneca

text: Men deserve praise for engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of producing any results.
author: Seneca

text: Why need we wonder if those who begin to climb a steep path do not succeed in ascending it very high? yet, if you be a man, look with respect on those who attempt great things, even though they fall.
author: Seneca

text: Whatever I may possess, I will neither hoard it greedily nor squander it recklessly.
author: Seneca

text: I will do nothing because of public opinion, but everything because of conscience: whenever I do anything alone by myself I will believe that the eyes of the Roman people are upon me while I do it.
author: Seneca

text: In eating and drinking my object shall be to quench the desires of Nature, not to fill and empty my belly.
author: Seneca

text: In fine, my riches belong to me, you belong to your riches.
author: Seneca

text: Cease, then, forbidding philosophers to possess money: no one has condemned wisdom to poverty.
author: Seneca

text: He who believes giving to be an easy matter, is mistaken: it offers very great difficulties, if we bestow our bounty rationally, and do not scatter it impulsively and at random.
author: Seneca

text: A benefit should be invested in the same manner as a treasure buried deep in the earth, which you would not dig up unless actually obliged.
author: Seneca

text: Riches, I say, are not a good thing; for if they were, they would make men good: now since that which is found even among bad men cannot be termed good, I do not allow them to be called so: nevertheless I admit that they are desirable and useful and contribute great comforts to our lives.
author: Seneca

text: I shall make whatever befals me become a good thing, but I prefer that what befals me should be comfortable and pleasant and unlikely to cause me annoyance: for you need not suppose that any virtue exists without labour, but some virtues need spurs, while others need the curb.
author: Seneca

text: The hardness of flint is known to none so well as to those who strike it.
author: Seneca

text: I offer myself to all attacks, like some lonely rock in a shallow sea, which the waves never cease to beat upon from whatever quarter they may come, but which they cannot thereby move from its place nor yet wear away, for however many years they may unceasingly dash against it.
author: Seneca

text: For the force of reason in disputation is to be sought after rather than authority, since the authority of the teacher is often a disadvantage to those who are willing to learn; as they refuse to use their own judgment, and rely implicitly on him whom they make choice of for a preceptor.
author: Cicero

text: If it is difficult to know all the doctrines of any one sect, how much more is it to know those of every sect! which, however, must necessarily be known to those who resolve, for the sake of discovering truth, to dispute for or against all philosophers without partiality.
author: Cicero

text: Do you suppose if beasts were endowed with reason that every one would not give the prize of beauty to his own species?
author: Cicero

text: Here I touch on a difficult point; for so great is the force of nature that there is no man who would not choose to be like a man, nor, indeed, any ant that would not be like an ant.
author: Cicero

text: The most curious inquirer cannot arrive at the knowledge of all those creatures which inhabit the earth, sea, fens, and rivers; and shall we deny the existence of them because we never saw them?
author: Cicero

text: Can there be any glory or excellence in that nature which only contemplates its own happiness, and neither will do, nor does, nor ever did anything?
author: Cicero

text: Is there no natural charity in the dispositions of good men?
author: Cicero

text: The best, the chastest, the most sacred and pious worship of the Gods is to reverence them always with a pure, perfect, and unpolluted mind and voice; for our ancestors, as well as the philosophers, have separated superstition from religion.
author: Cicero

text: We are the only animals who, from our knowledge of navigation, can manage what nature has made the most violent--the sea and the winds.
author: Cicero

text: Man alone of all animals has observed the courses of the stars, their risings and settings.
author: Cicero

text: Men do not store up corn for mice and ants, but for their wives, their children, and their families.
author: Cicero

text: There never, therefore, was a great man without divine inspiration.
author: Cicero

text: If a storm should damage the corn or vineyard of a person, or any accident should deprive him of some conveniences of life, we should not judge from thence that the Deity hates or neglects him.
author: Cicero

text: If folly, by the unanimous consent of philosophers, is allowed to be the greatest of all evils, and if no one ever attained to true wisdom, we, whom they say the immortal Gods take care of, are consequently in a state of the utmost misery.
author: Cicero

text: Many robbers have been executed; but the number of those who have suffered for their crimes is short of those whom they have robbed and murdered.
author: Cicero

text: When we are honored with new dignities, or blessed with increase of riches; when we are favored by fortune beyond our expectation, or luckily delivered from any approaching evil, we return thanks for it to the Gods, and assume no praise to ourselves. But who ever thanked the Gods that he was a good man?
author: Cicero

text: No one ever offered a tenth of his estate to Hercules to be made wise.
author: Cicero

text: It is universally agreed that good fortune we must ask of the Gods, but wisdom must arise from ourselves; and though temples have been consecrated to the Mind, to Virtue, and to Faith, yet that does not contradict their being inherent in us.
author: Cicero

text: If kings neglect anything, want of knowledge may be pleaded in their defence; but ignorance cannot be brought as an excuse for the Gods.
author: Cicero

text: I think that there is nothing, not even crime, more opposed to poetry, to philosophy, ay, to life itself, than this incessant business.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: If a man walk in the woods for love of them half of each day, he is in danger of being regarded as a loafer; but if he spends his whole day as a speculator, shearing off those woods and making earth bald before her time, he is esteemed an industrious and enterprising citizen.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: The ways by which you may get money almost without exception lead downward.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Those services which the community will most readily pay for, it is most disagreeable to render. You are paid for being something less than a man.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Do not hire a man who does your work for money, but him who does it for love of it.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: The community has no bribe that will tempt a wise man. You may raise money enough to tunnel a mountain, but you cannot raise money enough to hire a man who is minding his own business.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: I wish to suggest that a man may be very industrious, and yet not spend his time well. There is no more fatal blunderer than he who consumes the greater part of his life getting his living.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: If I should sell both my forenoons and afternoons to society, as most appear to do, I am sure, that for me there would be nothing left worth living for.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: You must get your living by loving.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: How can one be a wise man, if he does not know any better how to live than other men?—if he is only more cunning and intellectually subtle?
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: A grain of gold will gild a great surface, but not so much as a grain of wisdom.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: It is not enough to tell me that you worked hard to get your gold. So does the Devil work hard.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: A man had better starve at once than lose his innocence in the process of getting his bread.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: When our life ceases to be inward and private, conversation degenerates into mere gossip.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: You may depend on it, that the poor fellow who walks away with the greatest number of letters, proud of his extensive correspondence, has not heard from himself this long while.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: It requires more than a day’s devotion to know and to possess the wealth of a day.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: We do not live for idle amusement. I would not run round a corner to see the world blow up.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Really to see the sun rise or go down every day, so to relate ourselves to a universal fact, would preserve us sane forever.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: It is so hard to forget what it is worse than useless to remember!
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: I believe that the mind can be permanently profaned by the habit of attending to trivial things, so that all our thoughts shall be tinged with triviality.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Read not the Times. Read the Eternities.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Knowledge does not come to us by details, but in flashes of light from heaven.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: We should treat our minds, that is, ourselves, as innocent and ingenuous children, whose guardians we are, and be careful what objects and what subjects we thrust on their attention.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: What is it to be born free and not to live free? What is the value of any political freedom, but as a means to moral freedom?
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: In short, as a snow-drift is formed where there is a lull in the wind, so, one would say, where there is a lull of truth, an institution springs up. But the truth blows right on over it, nevertheless, and at length blows it down.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.
author: Buddha

text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
author: Buddha

text: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.
author: Buddha

text: As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.
author: Buddha

text: It is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to hold in and flighty, rushing wherever it listeth; a tamed mind brings happiness.
author: Buddha

text: Whatever a hater may do to a hater, or an enemy to an enemy, a wrongly-directed mind will do us greater mischief.
author: Buddha

text: Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.
author: Buddha

text: The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.
author: Buddha

text: If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.
author: Buddha

text: Do not have evil-doers for friends, do not have low people for friends: have virtuous people for friends, have for friends the best of men.
author: Buddha

text: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
author: Buddha

text: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
author: Buddha

text: If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good.
author: Buddha

text: Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.
author: Buddha

text: Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find.
author: Buddha

text: Bad deeds, and deeds hurtful to ourselves, are easy to do; what is beneficial and good, that is very difficult to do.
author: Buddha

text: He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.
author: Buddha

text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.
author: Buddha

text: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.
author: Buddha

text: From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear.
author: Buddha

text: He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.
author: Buddha

text: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
author: Buddha

text: There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.
author: Buddha

text: There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed.
author: Buddha

text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.
author: Buddha

text: A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned.
author: Buddha

text: If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great.
author: Buddha

text: Good people shine from afar, like the snowy mountains; bad people are not seen, like arrows shot by night.
author: Buddha

text: If anything is to be done, let a man do it, let him attack it vigorously! A careless pilgrim only scatters the dust of his passions more widely.
author: Buddha

text: An evil deed is better left undone, for a man repents of it afterwards; a good deed is better done, for having done it, one does not repent.
author: Buddha

text: The lover's ailment is different from all ailments; Love is the astrolabe of God's mysteries.
author: Rumi

text: However much we describe and explain love, When we fall in love we are ashamed of our words.
author: Rumi

text: If the saint handles earth, it becomes gold; If a sinner handles gold, it turns to dust.
author: Rumi

text: Patience will accomplish thy desire, not haste.
author: Rumi

text: Through love bitter things seem sweet, Through love bits of copper are made gold.
author: Rumi

text: Through love hard stones become soft as butter, Without love soft wax becomes hard iron.
author: Rumi

text: Wherever there is a pain there goes the remedy, Wherever there is poverty there goes relief.
author: Rumi

text: Seek not water, only show you are thirsty, That water may spring up all around you.
author: Rumi

text: Pain is a treasure, for it contains mercies; The kernel is soft when the rind is scraped off.
author: Rumi

text: The spring seasons are hidden in the autumns, And autumns are charged with springs; flee them not.
author: Rumi

text: He who accepts everything as true is a fool, But he who says all is false is a knave.
author: Rumi

text: Keep silence, that you may hear Him speaking Words unutterable by tongue in speech.
author: Rumi

text: Small knowledge has not the compass of great knowledge any more than a short year has the length of a long year.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Those who dream of the banquet, wake to lamentation and sorrow. Those who dream of lamentation and sorrow wake to join the hunt.
author: Zhuangzi

text: While they dream, they do not know that they dream.
author: Zhuangzi

text: By and by comes the Great Awakening, and then we find out that this life is really a great dream.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
author: Zhuangzi

text: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
author: Zhuangzi

text: When I first began to cut up bullocks, I saw before me simply whole bullocks. After three years' practice, I saw no more whole animals.
author: Zhuangzi

text: A good cook changes his chopper once a year,—because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month,—because he hacks.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The honours of this world are light as feathers, yet none estimate them at their true value. The misfortunes of this life are weighty as the earth itself, yet none can keep out of their reach.
author: Zhuangzi

text: All men know the use of useful things; but they do not know the use of useless things.
author: Zhuangzi

text: He who knows what God is, and who knows what Man is, has attained.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The pure men of old acted without calculation, not seeking to secure results. They laid no plans.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The pure men of old slept without dreams, and waked without anxiety.
author: Zhuangzi

text: A man who knows that he is a fool is not a great fool. A man who knows his error is not greatly in error.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The repose of the Sage is not what the world calls repose. His repose is the result of his mental attitude.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The mind of the Sage being in repose becomes the mirror of the universe, the speculum of all creation.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Those who make wealth their all in all, cannot bear loss of money. Those who make distinction their all in all, cannot bear loss of fame.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The snow-goose is white without a daily bath. The raven is black without daily colouring itself.
author: Zhuangzi

text: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,—the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,—the creature of a season.
author: Zhuangzi

text: He who clearly apprehends the scheme of existence, does not rejoice over life, nor repine at death; for he knows that terms are not final.
author: Zhuangzi

text: To know that failure is fate and that success is opportunity, and to remain fearless in great danger,—this is the courage of the Sage.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Those who understand the conditions of life devote no attention to things which life cannot accomplish. Those who understand the conditions of destiny devote no attention to things over which knowledge has no control.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Straight trees are the first felled. Sweet wells are soonest exhausted.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Life must bring us from somewhere, and death must carry us back.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Man passes through this sublunary life as a white horse passes a crack. Here one moment, gone the next.
author: Zhuangzi

text: The raison d'être of language is an idea to be expressed. When the idea is expressed, the language may be ignored.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Real friendship is unison without the aid of smiles.
author: Zhuangzi

text: Beside a river seat thee on the sward; It floweth past—so flows thy life away, So sweetly, swiftly, fleets our little day—Swift, but enough for me!
author: Hafiz

text: I have enough of loss, enough of gain; I have my Love, what more can I obtain?
author: Hafiz

text: A tale of April the meadows unfold—Ah, foolish for future credit to slave, And to leave the cash of the present untold!
author: Hafiz

text: Drunken am I, yet place not my name In the Book of Doom, nor pass judgment on it; Who knows what the secret finger of Fate Upon his own white forehead has writ!
author: Hafiz

text: If with tears, oh Hafiz, thine eyes are wet, Scatter them round thee like grain, and snare The Bird of Joy when it comes to thy net.
author: Hafiz

text: When pleasant hours slip from the hand of Fate, Reckon each hour as a certain gain; Who seeks to know the end of mortal care Shall question his experience in vain.
author: Hafiz

text: Thy fettered life hangs on a single thread—Some comfort for thy present ills devise, But those that time may bring thou shalt not dread.
author: Hafiz

text: Although His thrall shall miss the road and err, ’Tis but to teach him wisdom through distress, Else Pardon and Compassionate Mercy were But empty syllables and meaningless.
author: Hafiz

text: The span of thy life is as five little days, Brief hours and swift in this halting-place; Rest softly, ah rest! while the Shadow delays, For Time’s self is nought and the dial’s face.
author: Hafiz

text: Consider the rose that breaks into flower, Neither repines though she fade and die—The powers of the world endure for an hour, But nought shall remain of their majesty.
author: Hafiz

text: Lay not reproach at the drunkard’s door Oh Fanatic, thou that art pure of soul; Not thine on the page of life to enrol The faults of others!
author: Hafiz

text: Or less or more I have swerved from my path—keep thou to thine own! For every man when he reaches the goal Shall reap the harvest his hands have sown.
author: Hafiz

text: Alike the drunk and the strict of fare For his mistress yearns—in the mosque Love doth dwell And the church, for his lodging is everywhere.
author: Hafiz

text: The Sultan’s crown, with priceless jewels set, Encircles fear of death and constant dread; It is a head-dress much desired—and yet Art sure ’tis worth the danger to the head?
author: Hafiz

text: Ah, seek the treasure of a mind at rest And store it in the treasury of Ease; Not worth a loyal heart, a tranquil breast, Were all the riches of thy lands and seas!
author: Hafiz

text: Not all the changes that thy days unfold Shall rouse thy wonder; Time’s revolving sphere Over a thousand lives like thine has rolled.
author: Hafiz

text: Like Hafiz, drain the goblet cheerfully While minstrels touch the lute and sweetly sing, For all that makes thy heart rejoice in thee Hangs of Life’s single, slender, silken string.
author: Hafiz

text: The secret of the world thou shalt not learn, And yet behind the veil Love’s fire may burn—Weep’st thou? let hope return and weep no more!
author: Hafiz

text: To-day may pass, to-morrow pass, before The turning wheel give me my heart’s desire; Heaven’s self shall change, and turn not evermore The universal wheel of Fate in ire.
author: Hafiz

text: The goal lies far, and perilous is thy road, Yet every path leads to that same abode Where thou shalt drop thy load—oh, weep no more!
author: Hafiz

text: The long-drawn tyranny of grief shall pass, Parting shall end in meeting, the lament Of the sad bird that sang “Alas, alas!” Shall reach the rose in her red-curtained tent.
author: Hafiz

text: Dear is the rose—now, now her sweets proclaim, While yet the purple petals blush and blow; Hither adown the path of Spring she came, And by the path of Autumn she will go.
author: Hafiz

text: Hafiz, why art thou ever telling o’er The tale of absence and of sorrow’s night? Knowest thou not that parting goes before All meeting, and from darkness comes the light!
author: Hafiz

text: Seeing but himself, the Zealot sees but sin; Grief to the mirror of his soul let in, Oh Lord, and cloud it with the breath of sighs!
author: Hafiz

text: Give thanks for nights spent in good company, And take the gifts a tranquil mind may bring; No heart is dark when the kind moon doth shine, And grass-grown river-banks are fair to see.
author: Hafiz

text: And it shall be my endeavour to reveal thee in my actions, knowing it is thy power gives me strength to act.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Only let me make my life simple and straight, like a flute of reed for thee to fill with music.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Pride can never approach to where thou walkest in the clothes of the humble among the poorest, and lowliest, and lost.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee! He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: The traveller has to knock at every alien door to come to his own, and one has to wander through all the outer worlds to reach the innermost shrine at the end.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: My desires are many and my cry is pitiful, but ever didst thou save me by hard refusals; and this strong mercy has been wrought into my life through and through.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: I have had my invitation to this world’s festival, and thus my life has been blessed.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: The morning will surely come, the darkness will vanish, and thy voice pour down in golden streams breaking through the sky.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: My debts are large, my failures great, my shame secret and heavy; yet when I come to ask for my good, I quake in fear lest my prayer be granted.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: He whom I enclose with my name is weeping in this dungeon. I am ever busy building this wall all around; and as this wall goes up into the sky day by day I lose sight of my true being in its dark shadow.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: If I call not thee in my prayers, if I keep not thee in my heart, thy love for me still waits for my love.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Give me the strength lightly to bear my joys and sorrows.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Give me the strength never to disown the poor or bend my knees before insolent might.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: And when old words die out on the tongue, new melodies break forth from the heart; and where the old tracks are lost, new country is revealed with its wonders.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Tempest roams in the pathless sky, ships get wrecked in the trackless water, death is abroad and children play.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Thou hast brought the distant near and made a brother of the stranger.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: When one knows thee, then alien there is none, then no door is shut.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: The same stream of life that runs through my veins night and day runs through the world and dances in rhythmic measures.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Deliverance is not for me in renunciation. I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: From the words of the poet men take what meanings please them; yet their last meaning points to thee.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: On many an idle day have I grieved over lost time. But it is never lost, my lord.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Thy centuries follow each other perfecting a small wild flower.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: It is the pang of separation that spreads throughout the world and gives birth to shapes innumerable in the infinite sky.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: On the day when death will knock at thy door what wilt thou offer to him? Oh, I will set before my guest the full vessel of my life—I will never let him go with empty hands.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: I know that the day will come when my sight of this earth shall be lost, and life will take its leave in silence, drawing the last curtain over my eyes. Yet stars will watch at night, and morning rise as before, and hours heave like sea waves casting up pleasures and pains.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: We were neighbours for long, but I received more than I could give.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: I start on my journey with empty hands and expectant heart.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: And because I love this life, I know I shall love death as well.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: When I go from hence let this be my parting word, that what I have seen is unsurpassable.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: It was my songs that taught me all the lessons I ever learnt; they showed me secret paths, they brought before my sight many a star on the horizon of my heart.
author: Rabindranath Tagore

text: Riches are intended for the comfort of life, and not life for the purpose of hoarding riches.
author: Saadi

text: Two persons labored to a vain, and studied to an unprofitable end: he who hoarded wealth and did not spend it, and he who acquired science and did not practise it:--However much thou art read in theory, if thou hast no practice thou art ignorant.
author: Saadi

text: Three things have no durability without their concomitants: property without trade, knowledge without debate, or a sovereignty without government.
author: Saadi

text: Reveal not every secret you have to a friend, for how can you tell but that friend may hereafter become an enemy?
author: Saadi

text: Thou shouldst not utter a word in secret which thou wouldst not have spoken in the face of the public.
author: Saadi

text: Whoever despises a weak enemy resembles him who neglects a spark of fire:--To-day that thou canst quench it, put it out; for let fire rise into a flame, and it may consume a whole world.
author: Saadi

text: When irresolute in the despatch of business, incline to that side which is the least offensive:--Answer not with harshness a mild-spoken man, nor force him into war who knocks at the gate of peace.
author: Saadi

text: Were intellect to be annihilated from the face of the earth, nobody could be brought to say: "I am ignorant."
author: Saadi

text: Whoever does not do good, when he has the means of doing it, will suffer hardship when he has not the means:--None is more unlucky than the misanthrope, for on the day of adversity he has not a single friend.
author: Saadi

text: Life stands on the verge of a single breath; and this world is an existence between two nonentities.
author: Saadi

text: Whatever is produced in haste goes hastily to waste:--I have heard that, after a process of forty years, they convert the clay of the East into a China porcelain cup.
author: Saadi

text: A piece of crystal or glass is found everywhere, and held of no value; a ruby is obtained with difficulty, and therefore inestimable.
author: Saadi

text: Patience accomplishes its object, while hurry speeds to its ruin:--With my own eyes I saw in the desert that the deliberate man outstripped him that had hurried on.
author: Saadi
